decisions.location: Introduction, p. 5 (see also Abstract, p. 1, Sections II-III, pp. 6-11, and Conclusion Section IV, p. 12)
decisions.quote:
This test cannot be applied directly to the Cashflow 101 data set, which is the primary
data set in M&L, because the Cashflow 101 data set provided by M&L does not contain the
auction titles. Therefore, my primary empirical test does not apply directly to the primary results
in M&L. However, I discuss why wording differences may be important for this product as well.
I also argue that other results in M&L are consistent with search costs. One is that the
overbidding rate is higher among auctions with a larger spatial separation in search results from
the BIN. Search costs could generate this result because a larger separation would make it more
difficult to find both listings. I also apply my test to a new eBay data set of 552 new movie-DVD
auctions. I find significant overbidding here (23 percent of auctions), but a close connection
between wording and overbidding as well.
In summary, my reading of the evidence is that the auctions and low-price BINs
sometimes do not appear together on the same webpage. This is most clear for the M&L cross
decisions.reason: Across two distinct data streams—(1) reanalysis of Malmendier and Lee's (2011) shared data (Section II, where the cross section shows 60% vs. 37% overbidding by 'new' title wording, mean auction prices exceeding mean low BINs for only 22/88 products, and 150 item mismatches, while Cashflow 101 lacks auction titles so the primary wording test cannot be applied directly, alongside a corrected shipping-fee programming error in fn. 19) and (2) a new 552-auction eBay movie-DVD dataset (Section III)—Schneider statistically reproduces significant overbidding (23% of DVD auctions, with no decline across experience in fn. 20, though mean auction price is 18% below mean low BIN and overbidding is 35% vs. 15% by wording). However, his whole-target synthesis (Abstract, Introduction p. 5, Conclusion Section IV p. 12) is that M&L's key identifying assumption (that relevant auctions and low-price BINs appear on the same webpage with inconsequential search costs) may not hold—while noting alternative standard mechanisms (clarity in large result sets or seller-quality signaling)—so rejection of the standard model is premature and observed overbidding is not inconsistent with standard behavior once basic search costs are allowed (without claiming limited attention is absent, and noting an unedited apparent missing negation on raw p. 5).
